title: The brothers meet (Genesis 33)
hookLine: Esau runs to him, embraces him, and they weep

cards: A rehearsed speech. A gift sent ahead. A careful message to soften the landing.

That's how people get ready to face someone they hurt long ago and never made it right with, and Jacob has done all of it. Still limping from the river, he looks up and sees Esau coming, and the four hundred men with him.
He lines up his family, the ones he loves most at the very back, and walks out in front. As he comes closer, he bows to the ground, seven times. Years of dread, all in one walk across a field.

teach.b: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept." Ran. Jacob is inching forward, bowing.
Esau runs. The man Jacob feared most closes the distance himself. Then Jacob presses his gifts on him.
Esau says, I have enough, my brother; keep what you have. Jacob insists, and uses a telling word.
In Hebrew he says: take my blessing. Long ago he took Esau's blessing. Now he's trying to hand one back, and Esau takes it.
Look at the page: in a Torah scroll, the Hebrew word for and he kissed him has small dots written over its letters. The rabbis asked why, and they didn't agree.

One opinion in the midrash says the dots mean that this once, Esau's kiss was completely from the heart. Another says it wasn't a kiss at all, and reads it darkly. The dots stay on the page, and so do both readings.

teach.h: THEY WEEP, THEN PART IN PEACE.
teach.b: The brothers weep, and then they part.
Esau offers to travel together; Jacob politely puts him off and goes his own way. It's not a movie reunion where everyone moves in together.
It's two men who were enemies, who cried on each other's necks, and then lived at peace at a distance. Sometimes that's what repair looks like: not everything restored.
Just the running, the weeping, and a different road home.

how: The Mishnah teaches that Yom Kippur does not wipe away a wrong done to another person until that person is appeased, so in the days before it Jews are encouraged to go to the people they have wronged and ask forgiveness directly.

games.q: you're Esau. the brother who took your blessing long ago is walking toward you, bowing to the ground. you have four hundred men. what do you do?
o: make him come all the way to you.
run to meet him and embrace him.
games.why: "Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept." the one Jacob feared closes the distance himself.

practice: Let one face come to mind: someone you once wronged, not the worst thing you ever did, just a real one, and notice what you've carried about it, the dread, the shame, the speech you never gave.
Then picture one small step toward them: a message, a sentence that begins, I've been thinking about. You don't have to send it now, and they don't have to run to meet you.
